Crowds and healing do not confine the message to one town

By the evening of verse 33 the whole town is at the door. Jesus has healed many. Before dawn he leaves to pray alone (verse 35). The disciples find him and say everyone is looking for him. Verse 38 gives his answer: “Let’s go elsewhere.” He came to preach, and other towns have not heard. Success in one place does not decide where he goes next.
A blocked doorway leads into disputes about authority and need

Each scene in this chapter raises a complaint. Jesus forgives, eats with sinners, and does not have his disciples fast. The last complaint is about picking grain on the Sabbath. Verse 25 answers with David’s need and hunger. Verse 27 then states the purpose of the day. The Sabbath was made for people’s good. A rule about rest should not be turned against the hungry.
The question about saving life exposes the plan to destroy it

The watchers in verse 2 hope to accuse Jesus. Verse 4 puts a question to them with two pairs. Is the Sabbath for doing good or harm, for saving life or killing? They stay silent. He heals the man, which is the good. Verse 6 shows what they do on that same Sabbath. They go out and plan how to destroy him.
Questions about hearing become fear inside the boat

The disciples have spent the day hearing about trust in a hidden Kingdom. That night the waves break into the boat. Verse 38 gives their question: does he not care that they are dying? They doubt his concern, not his power. He stills the storm and asks why they have no faith (verse 40). Verse 41 says they were then even more afraid. They ask who this can be.
One healing interrupts another urgent request

A leader’s daughter is dying, and every moment counts. A woman in the crowd touches Jesus and is healed at once (verse 29). He could have kept walking. He stops and asks who touched him (verse 30). She comes forward in fear and tells him everything. Verse 34 calls her “Daughter” and sends her away in peace. She receives his attention as well as her cure, while Jairus waits.
The loaves should have changed the disciples' response to the sea

The disciples have just handed out bread to thousands (verses 41–43). Hours later they see Jesus on the water and cry out in fear. Verse 52 explains their reaction. They had not understood about the loaves. The feeding should have shown them who was with them. Their hearts were hardened. In Mark the people closest to Jesus are often slow to see.
A sacred gift claim can hide neglected parents

“Corban” in verse 11 means something pledged to God. A man could say this about the support he owed his parents. Verse 12 states the result. He is then not allowed to do anything for his father or mother. A religious vow cancels a plain commandment. Jesus says this makes God’s word void (verse 13). The example shows how piety can excuse neglect.
Partial sight stands beside partial understanding

This is the only healing in the Gospels done in two steps. After the first touch the man sees people like walking trees (verse 24). After the second he sees clearly (verse 25). Mark places the story between two scenes of poor sight. The disciples fail to understand the loaves (verses 17–21). Peter then names Jesus rightly and rejects his suffering (verses 29–32). Their sight is also partial.
The father's request admits the weakness that disciples conceal

The father’s cry in verse 24 holds two things together. He believes, and he knows his belief is weak. He says both aloud and asks for help. The disciples behave differently in this chapter. They do not understand and are afraid to ask (verse 32). They argue about rank and fall silent when questioned (verse 34). The father admits his weakness, and they hide theirs.
The same question reveals different desires in two requests

Jesus asks the same question twice in this chapter. In verse 36 he asks James and John what they want. They ask for the seats of honor. In verse 51 he asks a blind beggar. The beggar asks to see. One request seeks rank, and the other seeks sight. Verse 52 says the beggar then followed Jesus on the road.
The fig tree surrounds a dispute about the temple's purpose

Mark wraps the temple scene inside the fig tree story. The tree is cursed in verses 12–14 and found dead in verses 20–21. Between them Jesus stops the temple’s trade. Verse 17 quotes Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11. The house was meant for the prayer of all nations. A tree with leaves and no fruit frames that charge. The show of life without its purpose is what is judged.
The widow's whole living follows a warning about consumed houses

Verse 40 warns of scribes who “devour widows’ houses.” The next scene shows a widow at the treasury. Verse 44 says she gave everything she had to live on. Jesus praises the size of her gift measured by her means. The warning just before should stay in the reader’s mind. A system that takes a widow’s last coins is also in view. The next chapter opens with the temple’s coming ruin (13:2).
The warning to watch does not supply a predictable hour

The disciples ask for timing and a sign (verse 4). Verse 32 says no one knows the day, not even the Son. So the chapter cannot be used as a timetable. Verse 34 gives a different picture. A man leaves home and gives each servant his work. The doorkeeper is told to watch. The command to stay awake is a command to keep at one’s task.
The woman's understood gift contrasts with failed promises

Some at the table call the woman’s gift a waste (verses 4–5). Verse 8 gives Jesus’s reading of it. She has done what she could and prepared his body for burial. She alone acts as if his death is near. The disciples make promises in this chapter. Peter swears he will die before denying him (verse 31). By verse 50 they have all fled.
Mocked kingship becomes recognition beside the cross

Mockers tell Jesus to come down from the cross so they can believe (verse 32). He does not come down. Verse 39 says the officer saw how he died. The officer then calls him Son of God. This is the first human in Mark to say so. He is a foreign soldier at an execution. Recognition comes at the death, not through an escape from it.
The message names Peter after his denial and the disciples' flight

The disciples fled at the arrest (14:50). Peter denied Jesus three times (14:66–72). Verse 7 sends a message to “his disciples and Peter.” Peter is named on his own. The one who failed most publicly is not left out. The message also promises a meeting in Galilee, as Jesus said (14:28). The first word to those who ran is an invitation back.
